scenarios.title: Compounding demand
scenarios.premise: Suppose AI revenue keeps pace with spending: the leading labs' combined revenue run-rate more than doubles from about $100bn in late 2026 to over $200bn by the end of 2027 and the clouds' AI revenue grows 40% or more a year, so the hyperscalers raise capex from about $725-828bn in 2026 to over $1 trillion in 2027 and keep raising it through 2028, with chips, memory, packaging and power staying sold out.
signposts: The labs' combined run-rate passing $150bn during 2027
Hyperscalers guiding 2027 capex above $1 trillion
NVIDIA's data-centre revenue still rising quarter on quarter
HBM and CoWoS lead times lengthening rather than shortening
scenarios.reading: The scarcest inputs win most: ASML, TSMC, memory, power and NVIDIA keep pricing power, and the clouds earn back their capex. The labs grow in absolute terms but not against each other, since all of them ride the same wave. No one in the chain loses outright; the losers are relative, firms outside it that lose capital and attention.

scenarios.title: Capex digestion
scenarios.premise: Suppose AI revenue disappoints in 2027: the labs' run-rate growth slows to under 30% a year and enterprises cut pilots, so the hyperscalers cut capex by 30-40% from the 2026 level of about $725-828bn and hold it there for at least 18 months, as in past telecom and memory busts, while the Fed keeps rates near 4% and credit for data-centre builders tightens.
signposts: A hyperscaler cutting its 2027 capex guidance
GPU rental prices and HBM contract prices falling
Neocloud refinancing stress: CoreWeave's and Oracle's borrowing costs
Memory-maker shares falling on record earnings (SK Hynix fell 18.8% from 1 September 2026)
scenarios.reading: The scarcity premium reverses: the leveraged builders (CoreWeave, Oracle) and the labs with the largest commitments fall first, then memory and NVIDIA, whose $279bn of purchase commitments and customer financing become liabilities, and SoftBank with them. Cash-rich holders such as Berkshire gain the chance to buy; Apple, Visa, Walmart and Lilly are barely touched, and buyers get cheaper compute.

scenarios.title: The power wall
scenarios.premise: Suppose electricity, not chips or money, becomes the binding limit: grid connections in the main US markets take four years or more, large gas turbines are sold out to 2030 and the Hormuz disruption keeps gas and power prices high, so new data-centre capacity comes online 30-50% slower than planned through 2028 and firms that already own powered sites or their own generation are the only ones that can grow on schedule.
signposts: GE Vernova's gas backlog passing 130 GW, with delivery slots beyond 2030
Grid-connection waits for data centres in Virginia, Texas and Arizona
Wholesale power prices near data-centre clusters
Hyperscalers buying power plants or building their own generation
scenarios.reading: Advantage moves from chips to watts: nuclear owners (Constellation), turbine makers and whoever already holds powered capacity gain, including xAI, whose Colossus has its own power, and Berkshire through its utilities. Labs and GPU landlords that must buy new capacity lose time that money cannot buy back, and the server builders sell fewer racks.

scenarios.title: Taiwan disruption
scenarios.premise: Suppose a Chinese blockade or quarantine of Taiwan in 2027 halts most of TSMC's Taiwan output for six months or more: most of the world's leading-edge logic and advanced packaging stops, shipping and insurance to Taiwan freeze, and no other foundry can replace the lost volume for several years.
signposts: Chinese military exercises around Taiwan and war-risk insurance for shipping
The ramp of TSMC's fabs in Arizona and Japan
Intel's 18A and 14A winning outside customers
Governments stockpiling chips and packaging capacity
scenarios.reading: Everyone above TSMC loses, NVIDIA and Apple most, because the choke point has no substitute for years. Intel and Samsung gain as the only other leading-edge fabs, and China's own stack (SMIC, Huawei) gains relative ground. Firms that hold inventory or own their workloads survive; leveraged buyers of compute are in danger.

scenarios.title: Models commoditised
scenarios.premise: Suppose open-weight models (DeepSeek, Qwen and others) match each new frontier model within a few months and are served at a tenth of the price or less from 2027, while the closed labs' prices per token fall 70-90% a year, so model makers lose pricing power even though total use of AI keeps growing.
signposts: Open-weight models' benchmark scores against the frontier
The price per million tokens of the leading APIs
The labs' gross margins and enterprise churn
Usage share of Chinese open models outside China
scenarios.reading: The model stops being the toll-gate: DeepSeek and China's open-model ecosystem gain, and so do the buyers and firms that use AI rather than sell it. The closed labs and their financiers lose pricing power, and the GPU landlords that depend on them lose contracts. The big clouds and Apple are little changed: they sell whatever model wins.

scenarios.title: Regulatory clampdown
scenarios.premise: Suppose the US, the EU and several US states impose binding AI rules from 2027 (licensing and audits of frontier models, liability for harms, limits on training data and on data-centre power use) and antitrust remedies force the largest platforms to separate parts of their search, advertising, app-store or AI businesses, so frontier development slows and compliance costs billions a year.
signposts: Fines and obligations under the EU AI Act for general-purpose models
US federal or state bills licensing frontier models
Remedies in the US search and advertising antitrust cases
Moratoria or power-use rules for new data centres
scenarios.reading: Western rules and remedies slow the Western frontier: Alphabet, Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft face the costs and the break-ups, and the chain that sells to them slows. Labs outside the rules (DeepSeek, China) gain relative ground, as does Palantir, already built for government compliance.

scenarios.title: US-China decoupling
scenarios.premise: Suppose the US and China cut technology trade almost entirely from 2027 for at least three years: no US or allied chips, chipmaking tools, servicing, design software or cloud services sold to China; China bans US AI chips and restricts exports of rare earths and other critical minerals; and new legislation reimposes broad tariffs on Chinese goods.
signposts: New US rules on DUV servicing and memory-making tools
China's licences for rare-earth exports
Apple's and Tesla's sales in China
Huawei's Ascend shipments and SMIC's capacity
scenarios.reading: A full cutoff of tools and servicing hurts China's fabs (SMIC, CXMT) more than protection helps them, at least for two or three years, while Huawei holds. Firms that build or sell across the line (Apple, Foxconn, Tencent, BYD abroad) lose; Intel and TSMC gain as the West's fabs. Western toolmakers lose revenue but not position, and NVIDIA has already lost China.

scenarios.title: The market turns
scenarios.premise: Suppose that in 2027 the stock market turns as it did in 2000-2002: over 2027 and 2028 the price-to-earnings multiples of the most expensive companies fall by half or more, the equity window for loss-making companies closes for about 18 months, credit spreads widen and buybacks stop, while demand for AI keeps growing, but more slowly, at 20-30% a year.
signposts: Loss-making listings and late-stage private rounds pulled or repriced
Buyback authorisations suspended
Credit spreads on data-centre debt widening
The share of the S&P 500 in its ten largest companies falling
scenarios.reading: The share price stops working as a weapon. Companies that paid for growth with their valuation (the labs, SpaceX and xAI, CoreWeave, the richest multiples) must cut or sell themselves; those that fund themselves from profits (Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Berkshire, Walmart) buy what the others cannot afford, and the few end the bust holding more of the market than before. Written by the lead as an eighth world, after a critic noted that none of the seven closed the equity window.

archetypes-napoleon-grande-armee-corps.claim: The Grande Armée consisted, on formation, of six corps led by Napoleon's marshals and senior generals.

archetypes-napoleon-massed-artillery.claim: After 1807 Napoleon used massed artillery as a spearhead to pound a break in the enemy's line.

archetypes-napoleon-leipzig-1813.claim: The Sixth Coalition defeated Napoleon at Leipzig in October 1813.

archetypes-napoleon-waterloo-1815.claim: The Seventh Coalition defeated Napoleon at Waterloo in June 1815 and exiled him to Saint Helena.

quotes: The allies formed the Seventh Coalition, which defeated him at Waterloo in June 1815 and exiled him to the British island of Saint Helena, where he died in 1821.

archetypes-vienna-congress-dates.claim: The Congress of Vienna, chaired by Metternich, was held from September 1814 to June 1815.
archetypes-vienna-congress-dates.quote: The Congress was chaired by Austrian statesman Klemens von Metternich (Duke Metternich)  and was held in Vienna from September 1814 to June 1815.

archetypes-vienna-concert-of-europe.claim: The Vienna settlement gave birth to the Concert of Europe, which maintained the balance of powers until the First World War in 1914.
archetypes-vienna-concert-of-europe.quote: The Congress of Vienna settlement gave birth to the Concert of Europe, an international political doctrine that emphasized the maintaining of political boundaries, the balance of powers, and respecting spheres of influence and which guided foreign policy among the nations of Europe until the outbreak of the First World War in 1914.
quotes: The Congress of Vienna settlement gave birth to the Concert of Europe, an international political doctrine that emphasized the maintaining of political boundaries, the balance of powers, and respecting spheres of influence and which guided foreign policy among the nations of Europe until the outbreak of the First World War in 1914.

quotes: He formed his units into a giant wedge, with him leading the charge.

story-ai-flow-nvidia-3dfx-2000.reason: rejected by the skeptic: Wrong year. 15 December 2000 is the signing; the purchase closed on 18 April 2001. NVIDIA's 10-K405 for fiscal 2001: 'On April 18, 2001, our subsidiary completed the purchase contemplated by the definitive agreement. We have paid 3dfx approximately $70 million in total consideration.' Its 10-Q for the quarter to 29 April 2001: 'the cash consideration due at the closing was $70.0 million, less $15.0 million that was loaned to 3dfx pursuant to a Credit Agreement dated December 15, 2000', so $55 million moved in April 2001. The share consideration was contingent, and NVIDIA's 10-K for fiscal 2002 says 3dfx had not yet met the conditions for it. Re-add with period 2001 (or 2000-2001) from those filings.

story-ai-flow-intel-nvidia-licence-2011.reason: rejected by the skeptic: Wrong period. Intel's 10-K for 2011 (sec.gov, Note 17): 'We agreed to make payments totaling $1.5 billion to NVIDIA over six years ($300 million in each of January 2011, 2012, and 2013; and $200 million in each of January 2014, 2015, and 2016)'. So there were six installments over 2011-2016, not five ending in 2015. Drawn over 2011-2015, the January 2016 payment is lost and every year's rate is wrong. Re-add with period 2011-2016 from the 10-K.

quotes: Because the French involvement in the war was distant and naval in nature, over a billion livres tournois were spent by the French government to support the war effort, raising its overall debt to about 3.315 billion.

story-revolutions-chesapeake-french-flee.claim: At the Chesapeake de Grasse prepared 24 ships of the line to meet the British.
story-revolutions-chesapeake-french-flee.quote: De Grasse hastily prepared most of his fleet for battle—24 ships of the line—and sailed out to meet him.
quotes: De Grasse hastily prepared most of his fleet for battle—24 ships of the line—and sailed out to meet him.

story-revolutions-chesapeake-british-fle.claim: Graves sailed to the Chesapeake with 19 ships of the line.
story-revolutions-chesapeake-british-fle.quote: He sailed south from Sandy Hook, New Jersey, outside New York Harbor, with 19 ships of the line and arrived at the mouth of the Chesapeake early on 5 September to see de Grasse's fleet already at anchor in the bay.
quotes: He sailed south from Sandy Hook, New Jersey, outside New York Harbor, with 19 ships of the line and arrived at the mouth of the Chesapeake early on 5 September to see de Grasse's fleet already at anchor in the bay.

story-revolutions-yorktown-captured.claim: At Yorktown 8,000 soldiers and 214 artillery pieces were captured.
story-revolutions-yorktown-captured.quote: In all, 8,000 soldiers, 214 artillery pieces, thousands of muskets, 24 transport ships, wagons, and horses were captured.
quotes: In all, 8,000 soldiers, 214 artillery pieces, thousands of muskets, 24 transport ships, wagons, and horses were captured.

story-revolutions-treaty-paris-1783.claim: The Treaty of Paris was signed on 3 September 1783 by Adams, Franklin, Jay and Hartley.
story-revolutions-treaty-paris-1783.quote: The treaty was drafted on November 30, 1782,[a] and signed at the Hôtel d'York at present-day 56 Rue Jacob in Paris on September 3, 1783, by Adams, Franklin, Jay, and Hartley.
quotes: The treaty was drafted on November 30, 1782,[a] and signed at the Hôtel d'York at present-day 56 Rue Jacob in Paris on September 3, 1783, by Adams, Franklin, Jay, and Hartley.

story-revolutions-war-deaths.claim: More than 25,000 Patriots died during active military service.
story-revolutions-war-deaths.quote: More than 25,000 Patriots died during active military service.
quotes: More than 25,000 Patriots died during active military service.

story-revolutions-debt-service-1788.claim: By 1788 half of French state revenue went on servicing the monarchy's debt.
story-revolutions-debt-service-1788.unit: percent of revenue to debt service
story-revolutions-debt-service-1788.quote: Even after it ended, the monarchy continued to borrow heavily, and by 1788, half of state revenue went on servicing its debt.
quotes: Even after it ended, the monarchy continued to borrow heavily, and by 1788, half of state revenue went on servicing its debt.

story-revolutions-royal-household-1788.claim: Royal household spending in 1788 was 13% of total state expenses, excluding interest on debts.
story-revolutions-royal-household-1788.quote: Royal household spending in 1788 was 13% of total state expenses (excluding interest on debts).
quotes: Royal household spending in 1788 was 13% of total state expenses (excluding interest on debts).

story-revolutions-church-wealth-1789.claim: On the eve of the Revolution the Church held upwards of 7% of France's land and had yearly revenues of 150 million livres.
story-revolutions-church-wealth-1789.quote: At the eve of the revolution, the church possessed upwards of 7% of the country's land (figures vary) and generated yearly revenues of 150 million livres.
quotes: At the eve of the revolution, the church possessed upwards of 7% of the country's land (figures vary) and generated yearly revenues of 150 million livres.

story-revolutions-estates-population-178.claim: The Third Estate, doubled in 1789, represented about 98 percent of a population of roughly 28 million.
story-revolutions-estates-population-178.quote: The Third Estate representation was doubled, representing about 98 percent of the population of roughly 28 million.
quotes: The Third Estate representation was doubled, representing about 98 percent of the population of roughly 28 million.

story-revolutions-clergy-1789.claim: The First Estate represented 115,000 to 150,000 Catholic clergy, less than 1 per cent of the population.
story-revolutions-clergy-1789.unit: thousand clergy (115,000 to 150,000; the low end)
story-revolutions-clergy-1789.quote: The First Estate represented 115,000 to 150,000 Catholic clergy, less than 1 per cent of the population.
quotes: The First Estate represented 115,000 to 150,000 Catholic clergy, less than 1 per cent of the population.

story-revolutions-estates-deputies-1789.claim: The Estates-General of 1789 had 1,219 deputies: 302 for the clergy, 289 for the nobility and 611 for the Third Estate.
story-revolutions-estates-deputies-1789.quote: The number of deputies was 1,219 in total: 302 for the First Estate, 289 for the Second Estate and 611 for the Third Estate.
quotes: The number of deputies was 1,219 in total: 302 for the First Estate, 289 for the Second Estate and 611 for the Third Estate.

story-revolutions-europe-populations-179.claim: By the end of the 18th century France had 28 million people, against Britain's 12 million and Russia's 35 to 40 million.
story-revolutions-europe-populations-179.quote: France had the second-largest population in Europe by the end of the 18th century (28 million, as compared to Britain's 12 million and Russia's 35 to 40 million).
quotes: France had the second-largest population in Europe by the end of the 18th century (28 million, as compared to Britain's 12 million and Russia's 35 to 40 million).

story-revolutions-bastille-seven.claim: On 14 July 1789 the Bastille held only seven inmates when it was stormed.
story-revolutions-bastille-seven.quote: The prison contained only seven inmates at the time of its storming and was already scheduled for demolition but was seen by the revolutionaries as a symbol of the monarchy's abuse of power.
quotes: The prison contained only seven inmates at the time of its storming and was already scheduled for demolition but was seen by the revolutionaries as a symbol of the monarchy's abuse of power.

story-revolutions-church-property-1789.claim: On 2 November 1789 Church property held for revenue was nationalized and used as the backing for the assignats.
story-revolutions-church-property-1789.quote: On 2 November 1789, Catholic Church property that was held for purposes of church revenue was nationalized, and was used as the backing for the assignats.
quotes: On 2 November 1789, Catholic Church property that was held for purposes of church revenue was nationalized, and was used as the backing for the assignats.

story-revolutions-civil-constitution-bis.claim: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy fixed 83 bishops, one per department, in place of 135.
story-revolutions-civil-constitution-bis.quote: Under the Civil Constitution of the Clergy: There were 83 bishops, one per department, rather than the previous 135 bishops.
quotes: Under the Civil Constitution of the Clergy: There were 83 bishops, one per department, rather than the previous 135 bishops.

story-revolutions-louis-executed.claim: On 21 January 1793 Louis XVI, aged 38, was beheaded by guillotine on the Place de la Révolution.
story-revolutions-louis-executed.quote: On 21 January 1793, Louis XVI, at age 38, was beheaded by a guillotine on the Place de la Révolution.
quotes: On 21 January 1793, Louis XVI, at age 38, was beheaded by a guillotine on the Place de la Révolution.

story-revolutions-deficit-1789-1793.claim: Between 1789 and 1793 the annual deficit rose from 10% to 64% of gross national product.
story-revolutions-deficit-1789-1793.quote: Between 1789 and 1793, the annual deficit increased from 10% to 64% of gross national product, while annual inflation reached 3,500% after a poor harvest in 1794 and the removal of price controls.
quotes: Between 1789 and 1793, the annual deficit increased from 10% to 64% of gross national product, while annual inflation reached 3,500% after a poor harvest in 1794 and the removal of price controls.

story-revolutions-levee-en-masse-1793.claim: The Committee of Public Safety was formed on 6 April 1793 and the levée en masse drafted all men aged 18 to 25 into the army in August 1793.
story-revolutions-levee-en-masse-1793.quote: The Committee of Public Safety was formed (6 April 1793) and the levée en masse drafted all men aged 18 to 25 into the army (August 1793).
quotes: The Committee of Public Safety was formed (6 April 1793) and the levée en masse drafted all men aged 18 to 25 into the army (August 1793).

story-revolutions-first-coalition-1793.claim: In 1793 Austria, Sardinia, Naples, Prussia, Spain and Great Britain formed the First Coalition to curtail revolutionary France.
story-revolutions-first-coalition-1793.quote: In 1793, Austria, the Kingdom of Sardinia, the Kingdom of Naples, Prussia, the Kingdom of Spain, and the Kingdom of Great Britain formed the First Coalition to curtail the growing power of revolutionary France.
quotes: In 1793, Austria, the Kingdom of Sardinia, the Kingdom of Naples, Prussia, the Kingdom of Spain, and the Kingdom of Great Britain formed the First Coalition to curtail the growing power of revolutionary France.

story-revolutions-terror-death-sentences.claim: By the end of the Terror 16,594 official death sentences had been dispensed in France since June 1793, 2,639 of them in Paris.
story-revolutions-terror-death-sentences.quote: By then, 16,594 official death sentences had been dispensed throughout France since June 1793, of which 2,639 were in Paris alone.
quotes: By then, 16,594 official death sentences had been dispensed throughout France since June 1793, of which 2,639 were in Paris alone.

story-revolutions-terror-prairial.claim: Between 10 June and 27 July 1794, after the Law of 22 Prairial, another 1,366 were executed.
story-revolutions-terror-prairial.quote: Between 10 June and 27 July, another 1,366 were executed, causing fear among d'Herbois, Fouché and Tallien due to their past actions.
quotes: Between 10 June and 27 July, another 1,366 were executed, causing fear among d'Herbois, Fouché and Tallien due to their past actions.

story-revolutions-robespierre-executed.claim: By 2 p.m. Robespierre and twenty-one Robespierrists were sentenced to death under the law of 22 Prairial, without even a cursory hearing.
story-revolutions-robespierre-executed.quote: By 2 p.m., Robespierre and twenty-one "Robespierrists" faced accusations of counter-revolution and were sentenced to death under the provisions of the law of 22 Prairial, although without even a cursory hearing.
quotes: By 2 p.m., Robespierre and twenty-one "Robespierrists" faced accusations of counter-revolution and were sentenced to death under the provisions of the law of 22 Prairial, although without even a cursory hearing.

story-revolutions-coup-1799.claim: The bloodless coup of 18 Brumaire, on 9 November 1799, overthrew the Directory and replaced it with the French Consulate.
story-revolutions-coup-1799.quote: This bloodless coup d'état overthrew the Directory, replacing it with the French Consulate.
quotes: This bloodless coup d'état overthrew the Directory, replacing it with the French Consulate.
This occurred on 9 November 1799, which was 18 Brumaire, Year VIII, under the short-lived French Republican calendar system.

story-revolutions-plebiscite-1800.claim: The Consulate's constitution was approved by plebiscite on 7 February 1800.
story-revolutions-plebiscite-1800.quote: The constitution was approved by plebiscite on 7 February 1800.
quotes: The constitution was approved by plebiscite on 7 February 1800.

story-revolutions-plebiscite-1804.claim: The hereditary empire was confirmed by a plebiscite in June 1804: 3.5 million yes and 2,569 no officially, the yes count falsely inflated by 300,000 to 500,000.
story-revolutions-plebiscite-1804.quote: The hereditary empire was confirmed by a plebiscite in June.
quotes: The hereditary empire was confirmed by a plebiscite in June.
The official result showed 3.5 million voted "yes" and 2,569 voted "no".
The yes count, however, was falsely inflated by 300,000 to 500,000 votes.

story-revolutions-concordat-recognition.claim: In April 1802 Bonaparte celebrated peace and his Concordat of 1801, under which the pope recognized his regime and the regime recognized Catholicism as the majority religion.
story-revolutions-concordat-recognition.quote: In April, Bonaparte publicly celebrated the peace and his controversial Concordat of 1801 with Pope Pius VII under which the pope recognized Bonaparte's regime and the regime recognized Catholicism as the majority religion of France.
quotes: In April, Bonaparte publicly celebrated the peace and his controversial Concordat of 1801 with Pope Pius VII under which the pope recognized Bonaparte's regime and the regime recognized Catholicism as the majority religion of France.

story-revolutions-recognition-1804.claim: Britain, Russia, Sweden and the Ottoman Empire refused to recognize Napoleon's imperial title; Austria recognized it in return for his recognition of Francis I as Emperor of Austria.
story-revolutions-recognition-1804.quote: Britain, Russia, Sweden and the Ottoman Empire refused to recognize Napoleon's title.
quotes: Britain, Russia, Sweden and the Ottoman Empire refused to recognize Napoleon's title.
Austria, however, recognized Napoleon as Emperor of the French in return for his recognition of Francis I as Emperor of Austria.

story-revolutions-coronation-date.claim: Napoleon's coronation, with the participation of Pope Pius VII, took place at Notre Dame de Paris on 2 December 1804.
story-revolutions-coronation-date.quote: Napoleon's coronation, with the participation of Pope Pius VII, took place at Notre Dame de Paris on 2 December 1804.
quotes: Napoleon's coronation, with the participation of Pope Pius VII, took place at Notre Dame de Paris on 2 December 1804.

story-revolutions-coronation-ceremony.claim: Napoleon designed a new coronation ceremony, held at Notre-Dame in the presence of Pope Pius VII, unlike the sacre of the kings of France conferred by the archbishop of Reims.
story-revolutions-coronation-ceremony.quote: To this end, he designed a new coronation ceremony unlike that for the kings of France, which had emphasised the king's consecration (sacre) and anointment and was conferred by the archbishop of Reims in Reims Cathedral.[2] Napoleon's was a sacred ceremony held in the great cathedral of Notre-Dame de Paris in the presence of Pope Pius VII.
quotes: To this end, he designed a new coronation ceremony unlike that for the kings of France, which had emphasised the king's consecration (sacre) and anointment and was conferred by the archbishop of Reims in Reims Cathedral.[2] Napoleon's was a sacred ceremony held in the great cathedral of Notre-Dame de Paris in the presence of Pope Pius VII.

story-revolutions-grande-armee-1804.claim: The Grande Armée was formed in 1804 from the Army of England, a field army of over 100,000 men assembled for the invasion of the United Kingdom.
story-revolutions-grande-armee-1804.quote: The Grande Armée was formed in 1804 from the Armée des côtes de l'Océan (Army of the Ocean Coasts), more commonly referred to as the Armée d'Angleterre (Army of England), the French field army of over 100,000 men Napoleon had assembled for his planned invasion of the United Kingdom.
quotes: The Grande Armée was formed in 1804 from the Armée des côtes de l'Océan (Army of the Ocean Coasts), more commonly referred to as the Armée d'Angleterre (Army of England), the French field army of over 100,000 men Napoleon had assembled for his planned invasion of the United Kingdom.

story-revolutions-conscripts-1805-1813.claim: From 1805 to 1813 over 2.1 million Frenchmen were conscripted into the Imperial Army.
story-revolutions-conscripts-1805-1813.quote: In total, from 1805 to 1813, over 2.1 million Frenchmen were conscripted into the Imperial Army.
quotes: In total, from 1805 to 1813, over 2.1 million Frenchmen were conscripted into the Imperial Army.

story-revolutions-austerlitz-french-forc.claim: At Austerlitz Napoleon had some 72,000 men and 157 guns, against about 85,000 Allied soldiers, seventy percent of them Russian, and 318 guns.
story-revolutions-austerlitz-french-forc.quote: Napoleon had some 72,000 men and 157 guns for the impending battle, with about 7,000 troops under Davout still far to the south in the direction of Vienna.[73][74] The Allies had about 85,000 soldiers, seventy percent of them Russian, and 318 guns.
quotes: Napoleon had some 72,000 men and 157 guns for the impending battle, with about 7,000 troops under Davout still far to the south in the direction of Vienna.[73][74] The Allies had about 85,000 soldiers, seventy percent of them Russian, and 318 guns.

story-revolutions-austerlitz-allied-loss.claim: Allied casualties at Austerlitz stood at about 36,000 out of an army of 89,000, about 38% of their effective forces.
story-revolutions-austerlitz-allied-loss.quote: Allied casualties stood at about 36,000 out of an army of 89,000, representing about 38% of their effective forces.
quotes: Allied casualties stood at about 36,000 out of an army of 89,000, representing about 38% of their effective forces.

story-revolutions-trafalgar-fleet.claim: At Trafalgar Villeneuve fielded 33 ships of the line against Nelson.
story-revolutions-trafalgar-fleet.quote: Against Nelson, Vice-Admiral Villeneuve, sailing on his flagship Bucentaure, fielded 33 ships of the line, including some of the largest in the world at the time.
quotes: Against Nelson, Vice-Admiral Villeneuve, sailing on his flagship Bucentaure, fielded 33 ships of the line, including some of the largest in the world at the time.

story-revolutions-trafalgar-result.claim: At Trafalgar 18 French and Spanish ships were captured or destroyed while the British lost none.
story-revolutions-trafalgar-result.quote: 18 French and Spanish ships were ultimately captured or destroyed while the British lost none.
quotes: 18 French and Spanish ships were ultimately captured or destroyed while the British lost none.

story-revolutions-navy-expansion.claim: After 1793 Britain doubled its frigates, added 50 per cent more ships of the line and raised its sailors from 15,000 to 133,000 in eight years.
story-revolutions-navy-expansion.quote: Britain used its economic power to expand the Royal Navy, doubling the number of frigates, adding 50 per cent more large ships of the line, and increasing the number of sailors from 15,000 to 133,000 in eight years after the war began in 1793.
quotes: Britain used its economic power to expand the Royal Navy, doubling the number of frigates, adding 50 per cent more large ships of the line, and increasing the number of sailors from 15,000 to 133,000 in eight years after the war began in 1793.

story-revolutions-berlin-decree.claim: The Continental System, a large-scale embargo of Britain, ran from the Berlin Decree of 21 November 1806 until 11 April 1814.
story-revolutions-berlin-decree.quote: The French Empire in 1812 Directly administered Client states Continental System The Continental System or Continental Blockade (French: Blocus continental ) was a large-scale embargo by French emperor Napoleon I against the British Empire from 21 November 1806 until 11 April 1814, during the Napoleonic Wars.
quotes: The French Empire in 1812 Directly administered Client states Continental System The Continental System or Continental Blockade (French: Blocus continental ) was a large-scale embargo by French emperor Napoleon I against the British Empire from 21 November 1806 until 11 April 1814, during the Napoleonic Wars.

story-revolutions-system-weakened-coalit.claim: The loss of Britain as a trading partner also hit the economies of France and its allies, and angry governments ignored the system.
story-revolutions-system-weakened-coalit.quote: The loss of Britain as a trading partner also hit the economies of France and its allies.[7] Angry governments gained an incentive to ignore the Continental System, which led to the weakening of Napoleon's coalition.
quotes: The loss of Britain as a trading partner also hit the economies of France and its allies.[7] Angry governments gained an incentive to ignore the Continental System, which led to the weakening of Napoleon's coalition.

story-revolutions-second-coalition-1798.claim: A Second Coalition was formed in 1798 by Great Britain, Austria, Naples, the Ottoman Empire, the Papal States, Portugal, Russia and Sweden.
story-revolutions-second-coalition-1798.quote: A Second Coalition was formed in 1798 by Great Britain, Austria, Naples, the Ottoman Empire, the Papal States, Portugal, Russia, and Sweden.
quotes: A Second Coalition was formed in 1798 by Great Britain, Austria, Naples, the Ottoman Empire, the Papal States, Portugal, Russia, and Sweden.

story-revolutions-third-coalition-1805.claim: Britain allied with Austria, Russia and minor powers to form the Third Coalition in April 1805.
story-revolutions-third-coalition-1805.quote: After minor campaigns, Britain allied with Austria, Russia, and minor powers, to form the Third Coalition in April 1805.
quotes: After minor campaigns, Britain allied with Austria, Russia, and minor powers, to form the Third Coalition in April 1805.

story-revolutions-fourth-coalition-1806.claim: Prussia joined Britain and Russia in the Fourth Coalition, which resumed war in October 1806.
story-revolutions-fourth-coalition-1806.quote: Concerned about increasing French power, Prussia joined Britain and Russia in the Fourth Coalition, which resumed war in October 1806.
quotes: Concerned about increasing French power, Prussia joined Britain and Russia in the Fourth Coalition, which resumed war in October 1806.

story-revolutions-fifth-coalition-1809.claim: Austria re-entered the conflict and formed the Fifth Coalition in April 1809 with Spain and Britain.
story-revolutions-fifth-coalition-1809.quote: The diversion of French armies to the large new Anglo-Spanish front led to Austria reentering the conflict and forming the Fifth Coalition in April 1809, composed of Austria, Spain, and Britain.
quotes: The diversion of French armies to the large new Anglo-Spanish front led to Austria reentering the conflict and forming the Fifth Coalition in April 1809, composed of Austria, Spain, and Britain.

story-revolutions-jena-prussian-army.claim: The Prussian army awaiting Napoleon's advance in 1806 was a force of about 130,000 Prussians and 20,000 Saxons.
story-revolutions-jena-prussian-army.unit: thousand Prussian troops (the field force awaiting Napoleon; 20,000 Saxons besides)
story-revolutions-jena-prussian-army.quote: The Prussian army, meanwhile, awaited Napoleon's advance with a force composed of about 130,000 Prussians and 20,000 Saxons.
quotes: The Prussian army, meanwhile, awaited Napoleon's advance with a force composed of about 130,000 Prussians and 20,000 Saxons.

story-revolutions-jena-french-force.claim: At Jena Napoleon's force grew from 48,000 to 96,000 men, though only 40,000 took part in the battle against the Prussians.
story-revolutions-jena-french-force.quote: Initially 48,000 strong, the Emperor took advantage of his carefully planned and flexible dispositions to rapidly achieve local superiority, with a force reaching 96,000 men.[18] However, less than half fought the Prussians as only 40,000 men were sent and actually took part in the battle.
quotes: Initially 48,000 strong, the Emperor took advantage of his carefully planned and flexible dispositions to rapidly achieve local superiority, with a force reaching 96,000 men.[18] However, less than half fought the Prussians as only 40,000 men were sent and actually took part in the battle.

story-revolutions-spain-1808.claim: In November 1808 Napoleon's Armée d'Espagne of 278,670 men faced 80,000 raw, disorganized Spanish troops on the Ebro.
story-revolutions-spain-1808.quote: With his Armée d'Espagne of 278,670 men drawn up on the Ebro, facing 80,000 raw, disorganized Spanish troops,[58] Napoleon and his marshals carried out a massive double envelopment of the Spanish lines in November 1808.
quotes: With his Armée d'Espagne of 278,670 men drawn up on the Ebro, facing 80,000 raw, disorganized Spanish troops,[58] Napoleon and his marshals carried out a massive double envelopment of the Spanish lines in November 1808.

story-revolutions-austria-subsidy-1809.claim: Britain gave Austria £250,000 in silver for the 1809 war, with a further £1 million promised.
story-revolutions-austria-subsidy-1809.quote: Austria received £250,000 in silver, with a further £1 million promised for future expenses.
quotes: Austria received £250,000 in silver, with a further £1 million promised for future expenses.

story-revolutions-russia-initial-force.claim: Napoleon's initial force entering Russia exceeded 450,000 men, over 150,000 horses, about 25,000 wagons and nearly 1,400 guns.
story-revolutions-russia-initial-force.quote: Napoleon's initial force upon entering Russia exceeded 450,000 men,[31] over 150,000 horses,[32] approximately 25,000 wagons, and nearly 1,400 artillery pieces.
quotes: Napoleon's initial force upon entering Russia exceeded 450,000 men,[31] over 150,000 horses,[32] approximately 25,000 wagons, and nearly 1,400 artillery pieces.

story-revolutions-russia-deployed-600k.claim: In total, excluding Austrian and Prussian contingents, Napoleon deployed 600,000 soldiers against Russia, only half of them from France.
story-revolutions-russia-deployed-600k.quote: In total (excluding the separate Austrian and Prussian contingents), Napoleon deployed 600,000 soldiers, only half of whom were from France.
quotes: In total (excluding the separate Austrian and Prussian contingents), Napoleon deployed 600,000 soldiers, only half of whom were from France.

story-revolutions-russia-survivors.claim: Of an original force of 615,000, only 110,000 survivors stumbled back; Napoleon lost more than 500,000 men in Russia.
story-revolutions-russia-survivors.quote: Napoleon lost more than 500,000 men in Russia.[208] Out of an original force of 615,000, only 110,000 frostbitten and half-starved survivors stumbled back.
quotes: Napoleon lost more than 500,000 men in Russia.[208] Out of an original force of 615,000, only 110,000 frostbitten and half-starved survivors stumbled back.

story-revolutions-russia-army-peak-1812.claim: Drafting large numbers of reinforcements brought the Russian army to its peak 1812 strength of 904,000, with perhaps 100,000 near Moscow.
story-revolutions-russia-army-peak-1812.quote: By this point the Russians had managed to draft large numbers of reinforcements (volunteers) into the army, bringing the Russian army to their peak 1812 strength of 904,000, with perhaps 100,000 in the vicinity of Moscow.
quotes: By this point the Russians had managed to draft large numbers of reinforcements (volunteers) into the army, bringing the Russian army to their peak 1812 strength of 904,000, with perhaps 100,000 in the vicinity of Moscow.

story-revolutions-leipzig-scale.claim: The Battle of Leipzig involved about 560,000 soldiers, 2,200 guns and 133,000 casualties.
story-revolutions-leipzig-scale.quote: The battle was the culmination of the German campaign of 1813 and involved about 560,000 soldiers, 2,200 artillery pieces, the expenditure of 400,000 rounds of artillery ammunition, and 133,000 casualties.
quotes: The battle was the culmination of the German campaign of 1813 and involved about 560,000 soldiers, 2,200 artillery pieces, the expenditure of 400,000 rounds of artillery ammunition, and 133,000 casualties.

story-revolutions-leipzig-coalition.claim: At Leipzig the Coalition armies of Austria, Prussia, Sweden and Russia decisively defeated Napoleon's Grande Armée.
story-revolutions-leipzig-coalition.quote: The Coalition armies of Austria, Prussia, Sweden, and Russia, led by Tsar Alexander I, Karl von Schwarzenberg, Gebhard von Blücher and Swedish Crown Prince Charles John, decisively defeated the Grande Armée of French Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte.
quotes: The Coalition armies of Austria, Prussia, Sweden, and Russia, led by Tsar Alexander I, Karl von Schwarzenberg, Gebhard von Blücher and Swedish Crown Prince Charles John, decisively defeated the Grande Armée of French Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte.

story-revolutions-sixth-coalition-losses.claim: The Grand Army lost at least 370,000 casualties in the Russian campaign, with 200,000 captured.
story-revolutions-sixth-coalition-losses.quote: Total losses of the Grand Army were at least 370,000 casualties as a result of fighting, starvation and the freezing weather conditions, and 200,000 captured.
quotes: Total losses of the Grand Army were at least 370,000 casualties as a result of fighting, starvation and the freezing weather conditions, and 200,000 captured.

story-revolutions-britain-subsidy-peak.claim: British subsidies paid for a large proportion of the Austrian and Russian soldiers, peaking at about 450,000 in 1813.
story-revolutions-britain-subsidy-peak.quote: In terms of soldiers the French numerical advantage was offset by British subsidies that paid for a large proportion of the Austrian and Russian soldiers, peaking at about 450,000 in 1813.
quotes: In terms of soldiers the French numerical advantage was offset by British subsidies that paid for a large proportion of the Austrian and Russian soldiers, peaking at about 450,000 in 1813.

story-revolutions-britain-subsidies-tota.claim: Total cash subsidies to Britain's allies came to £46,289,549 from 1793 to 1814.
story-revolutions-britain-subsidies-tota.quote: Total cash subsidies to Britain's allies came out to £46,289,549 from 1793 to 1814.
quotes: Total cash subsidies to Britain's allies came out to £46,289,549 from 1793 to 1814.

story-revolutions-britain-budget-1814.claim: In 1814 the British budget included £10 million for the Allies and £38 million as interest on the national debt.
story-revolutions-britain-budget-1814.quote: The British budget in 1814 reached £66 million, including £10 million for the Navy, £40 million for the Army, £10 million for the Allies, and £38 million as interest on the national debt.
quotes: The British budget in 1814 reached £66 million, including £10 million for the Navy, £40 million for the Army, £10 million for the Allies, and £38 million as interest on the national debt.

story-revolutions-britain-debt.claim: Britain's national debt soared to £679 million, more than double GDP, and the whole cost of the war came to £831 million.
story-revolutions-britain-debt.quote: The national debt soared to £679 million, more than double the GDP.

story-revolutions-flow-britain-prussia-1.claim: Lord Castlereagh told the Commons on 26 May 1815 that Britain's subsidy of 1,800,000l. to Prussia in 1794, for 60,000 men, came to 30l. a man.

story-revolutions-flow-britain-prussia-1.reason: rejected by the skeptic: Not what Britain paid. The figure is Castlereagh's comparison in 1815 (1,800,000l. for 60,000 men, 30l. a man), recalled 21 years later: the treaty's yearly cost, not a payment. The Hague treaty of 19 Apr 1794 promised £300,000 and then 50,000 a month for 62,400 men (Britannica); Britain repudiated it in October 1794 (napoleon.org, Haugwitz). Sheridan's Commons motion (reported March 1795) put what Prussia had received at 'twelve hundred thousand pounds, and upwards'. The page of story-revolutions-britain-subsidies-total gives Prussia 3.1 million for all of 1793-1814, which 1.8M plus 1813's 666,666 plus a third of 1814 would exceed. A sum paid in 1794 (about 1.2 million) needs its own source.

As part of the deal, the U.S. assumed responsibility for up to 20 million francs ($3.75 million) of French debts owed to U.S. citizens. The remaining 60 million francs ($11.25 million) were financed through U.S. government bonds carrying 6% interest, redeemable between 1819 and 1822.
story-revolutions-flow-louisiana-purchas.reason: rejected by the skeptic: The price, not a flow from the United States to France. Of the 80 million francs, 20 million were French debts to US citizens that the United States took over and paid at home. The other 60 million were US 6% bonds, which France sold to Barings and Hope for 52 million francs, paid July 1803 to April 1804 (the same page); the United States repaid the bondholders in 1819-1822. No 80 million francs moved from the United States to France in 1803. As flows it needs those parts as their own facts (the bankers to France, 52 million, 1803-1804).

story-revolutions-flow-britain-russia-te.reason: rejected by the skeptic: A rate offered, not an amount paid: the quote says Britain 'offered to pay 1,250,000 pounds a year for every 100,000 troops'. No gated fact gives the troops it paid for or what was paid before Austerlitz (2 Dec 1805), so a flow would invent its amount (total: false, a unit per 100,000 troops). True as a term of the Third Coalition: re-add it as a term or a moment's fact, not a flow, if wanted.

story-revolutions-flow-prussia-tribute-1.claim: On 9 March 1808 France fixed the tribute to be levied from Prussia at 154,500,000 francs, deducting 53,500,000 already raised during the French occupation, and the sum was lowered in two steps to 120 million francs by 1 November 1808.

story-revolutions-flow-prussia-tribute-1.reason: rejected by the skeptic: Wrong years. 1808 is when the sum was fixed (lowered to 120 million francs by 1 Nov 1808), not when it was paid, and the page gives no payment dates. The Convention of Paris (8 Sep 1808) left French garrisons in Glogau, Stettin and Küstrin until the debt was discharged, so payments ran past 1808. Drawn as 120 million francs in 1808 alone, it puts several years' payments into one. The 53.5 million raised during the occupation (1806-1808) also moved and is outside the figure. Needs a payment schedule.

story-revolutions-flow-france-indemnity-.reason: rejected by the skeptic: Outside the story and without a payer actor. Payment began on 1 Dec 1815 (the first of the fifteen bonds was due 31 Mar 1816): after the story's end (1815) and after the seventh-coalition actor's end (1815-11), and from is null. The 700 million over 1815-1820 is the treaty's schedule, not what happened: at Aix-la-Chapelle (1818) 332 million were still owed and France paid 265 million for them, the occupation ending 30 Nov 1818, so about 633 million were paid, and not to 1820.
